p.scope-of-this-document: **Scope of this document.** The design forks a namespace author faces, each with its options, the choice this practice recommends, and the reasoning — so a future designer need not re-litigate settled ground.

p.four-forks: Four forks: flat versus grouped, enforce versus recommend, where short names live, and rename as alias versus new identity.

p.protocol-document-pointer: The laws these forks produce are in [`QUALIFIED-NAMING-PROTOCOL.md`](QUALIFIED-NAMING-PROTOCOL.md).

p.fork-1-question: The root fork: is an artifact addressed by a bare `name` unique across the whole registry, or by a `group`-qualified coordinate?

p.both-models-shipped-at-scale: Both models shipped at scale, so the trade is empirical, not theoretical:

td.fact: high — names are a finite commons
low — squatting is local to a group
per-artifact — the name names no owner
per-group — a group maps to an owner
a group must be chosen up front

p.flat-systems-bought-ergonomics-and-paid-: **What each bought and paid.** Flat systems bought day-one ergonomics and paid with a squatting arms race and a trust vacuum — `serde` reads clean, but nothing in the coordinate tells you *who* stands behind it, and two deep dependencies wanting the same bare name cannot both be satisfied.

p.grouped-systems-paid-verbosity-and-bough: Grouped systems paid verbosity up front — nobody enjoys typing `org.apache.commons` — and bought it back twice: a group maps to an owner (so trust is delegated wholesale, not re-earned per artifact), and group-qualified coordinates compose without collision at any depth.

p.the-verbosity-is-real-but-bounded: The verbosity is real but bounded, and Fork 3 buys most of it back with a short name at the human boundary.

p.SQUATTING-AND-TRUST-PROPERTIES-ARE-STRUC: The squatting and trust properties are structural — they cannot be patched onto a flat namespace after the fact.

p.npm-conceded-the-point-with-scope: npm itself conceded the point by bolting on `@scope/` once flat names ran out; starting grouped avoids the migration.

enforce-vs-recommend.title: Fork 2 — enforce style versus recommend it

p.fork-2-question: Given a group grammar, how hard does the core enforce the reverse-FQDN *convention*?

item.OPTION-A-ENFORCE: **Option A — enforce.** Require the group to be a domain the publisher provably controls (DNS check, TXT record, the works).

item.OPTION-B-RECOMMEND: **Option B — recommend.** Enforce only the *grammar* (lowercase, dot-separated segments) and the *uniqueness* of the group; leave reverse-FQDN as a convention for humans and linters.

p.reverse-fqdn-piggybacks-on-dns-uniquenes: Reverse-FQDN is worth recommending because it piggybacks on DNS's existing global uniqueness — the trick Sun adopted for Java packages in 1995 — so two independent authors almost never collide by accident.

p.enforcing-domain-ownership-buys-little-a: But enforcing domain ownership buys little and costs a lot: it couples publishing to DNS administration, breaks for internal registries with no public domain, and still does not stop a determined bad actor who *does* own a domain.

p.THE-RESOLVERS-JOB-IS-NARROW: The resolver's job is narrow — check grammar, check uniqueness — and taste is left to linters.

p.maven-made-the-same-call: Maven made the same call: it recommends reverse-FQDN groupIds and enforces none of it.

p.THE-GRAMMAR-IS-THE-CONTRACT-THE-STYLE-IS: The grammar is the contract; the style is guidance.

short-names.title: Fork 3 — where do short names live

p.fork-3-question: If a short name is a convenience, *how much* of the system may see it?

item.OPTION-EVERYWHERE: **Everywhere.** Short names are first-class: manifests, lockfiles, and dependency edges may all carry them.

item.OPTION-NOWHERE: **Nowhere.** Ban short names entirely; humans type fully-qualified coordinates always.

item.OPTION-CLI-BOUNDARY-ONLY: **CLI boundary only.** Short names are legal solely as human-typed CLI input, resolved once, and never persisted.

p.everywhere-re-imports-the-transitive-col: "Everywhere" re-imports the flat namespace's transitive-collision problem: a short name buried in a transitive manifest is ambiguous at a point where no human is present to disambiguate it.

p.nowhere-throws-away-the-ergonomic-win: "Nowhere" is collision-safe but throws away the entire ergonomic win of Fork 1's concession — nobody wants to type `org.example.tools/widget` at a prompt.

p.BOUNDARY-ONLY-IS-THE-SWEET-SPOT: "Boundary only" is the sweet spot, and its property is decisive: short-name resolution happens *once*, for a human's argument, against an index — then the qualified form is stored.

p.A-SHORT-NAME-NEVER-RECURSES-INTO-THE-GRA: Because persisted state is qualified-only, the dependency graph is built entirely from qualified names, and **a short name never recurses into the graph**.

p.TRANSITIVE-COLLISIONS-BECOME-IMPOSSIBLE-: Transitive collisions become impossible by construction rather than by a runtime check.

p.this-is-the-cargo-npm-split-generalised: This is exactly the cargo/npm split — `add serde` on the command line, `serde = "1"` in the manifest — generalised into a law.

rename.title: Fork 4 — rename: alias table versus new identity

p.an-author-wants-to-rename-a-published-pa: An author wants to rename a published package.

item.OPTION-ALIAS-TABLE: **Alias table.** Keep a mapping `old → new`; resolve the old coordinate to the new artifact so existing consumers keep working.

item.OPTION-NEW-IDENTITY: **New identity.** Treat the renamed package as a genuinely new package: it starts a fresh version line, and the old coordinate is frozen (yanked or left as-is), never repointed.

p.the-alias-table-is-seductive-but-re-intr: The alias table is seductive — it seems to spare consumers a migration — but it re-introduces precisely the ambiguity groups were built to remove.

p.under-an-alias-every-reader-must-consult: Under an alias, two coordinates now name one artifact, and every reader must consult the mapping to know that `old/foo` and `new/foo` are the same bytes.

p.trust-stops-being-delegable-under-an-ali: Trust stops being delegable: the coordinate no longer tells the whole truth about ownership, because the *real* owner is one hop away through a table the reader must know exists.

p.NEW-IDENTITY-KEEPS-EVERY-COORDINATE-HONE: New identity keeps every coordinate honest.

p.A-CHANGED-TUPLE-IS-A-CHANGED-IDENTITY: Identity is the tuple `(group, name, version, content-hash)`; change the group or name and the tuple changed, so the identity changed — this is a consequence of the identity law, not an extra rule.

p.THE-OLD-COORDINATE-STAYS-WELDED-TO-ITS-B: The old `name@version` stays welded to the bytes it always meant (no coordinate is *ever* reused for different content), and the new name earns its own history from `0.1.0` forward.

p.A-CONSUMER-MIGRATES-DELIBERATELY: A consumer migrates deliberately, by editing a qualified name they can see — not silently, through a redirect they cannot.

item.SUM-FLAT-VS-GROUPED: **Flat vs grouped → grouped.** Verbosity is bounded and bought back at the boundary; squatting-resistance and delegated trust are structural and cannot be retrofitted onto flat names.

item.SUM-WHERE-SHORT-NAMES-LIVE: **Where short names live → CLI boundary only.** Resolved once against an index, then stored qualified — which is what makes transitive collisions impossible.

item.SUM-RENAME-IS-A-NEW-IDENTITY: **Rename → new identity, not alias.** An alias re-introduces the ambiguity groups removed; a new identity keeps every coordinate honest and every version line attached to the bytes it named.
